`Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Proxy-Authenticate`, `Proxy-Authorization`, `TE`, `Trailer`, `Transfer-Encoding`, and `Upgrade` are stripped from both the outbound request and the inbound response, along with every header listed in the `Connection` field per RFC 9110 §7.6.1. This prevents request smuggling (`TE`/`Transfer-Encoding`), proxy-credential forwarding, and protocol-upgrade leaks. A request whose `Connection` fields list more than 32 names is refused with `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` before it is forwarded, and an upstream response that does is answered with `502 Bad Gateway`, since each name costs a pass over every header line. Where header names are kept as sent (`DisableHeaderNormalizing` for the request, a client with `DisableHeaderNamesNormalizing` for the response), further spellings of a removed name count toward the same 32: every spelling besides the one listed in `Connection` or the standard one, except that on the response the standard names share one free spelling each, whichever name uses it. `Balancer`, `Forward`, `DomainForward`, and `BalancerForward` likewise answer `431` to a request that spells `X-Real-IP` in more than 32 ways besides `X-Real-IP`, since they replace every one of them. The legacy `KeepConnectionHeader` option preserves only the literal `Connection` header for backwards compatibility; the other hop-by-hop headers are still stripped. To preserve every hop-by-hop header (not recommended), set `SecurityPolicy.KeepHopByHopHeaders = true`.

-The fields a client sends in the trailer section of a chunked request are dropped together with `Trailer`, as [RFC 9112 §7.1.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-7.1.2) lets a recipient that removes the chunked coding do, instead of reaching the upstream as header lines: whatever screened the header section in front of this hop never saw them. Fiber drops them as the request arrives or, for a body streamed with `StreamRequestBody`, once that body has been read, including while the proxy forwards it. A header line sharing a name with a trailer field is kept. A streamed body whose trailer section names more than 16 fields also fails to read, which answers a request whose body the proxy reads with `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`. The trailer section of an upstream's chunked response is dropped the same way, whether its fields were announced in `Trailer` or not: the proxy answers with a sized body, which carries no trailer section, and a recipient must not merge trailer fields into the header section ([RFC 9110 §6.5.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-6.5.1)); a response whose trailer section names more than 16 fields is answered with `502 Bad Gateway`. The section is gone before `ModifyResponse` runs and before `Do` or `Forward` return, so neither a hook nor a handler reads a trailer field of the upstream's response. All of this holds with `KeepHopByHopHeaders` set.

A client that streams response bodies (`StreamResponseBody`, or a response whose `StreamBody` is set) receives the section only once the body has been read, after that point; the proxy reads such a body from a response of its own, which keeps the section, so it reaches neither the hook nor the client. All of this holds with `KeepHopByHopHeaders` set.

The names a client lists in `Connection` are removed from the request as it was received, with one intentional exception to RFC 9110 §7.6.1: the forwarding headers `X-Real-IP`, `Forwarded`, and every `X-Forwarded-*` header stay. They tell the upstream about the client as this hop saw it, and an upstream that trusts the gateway acts on them, so they are the gateway's to write and not the client's to have removed. `Balancer`, `Forward`, `DomainForward`, and `BalancerForward` write `X-Real-IP` only after the listing has been applied, and the exception also covers a forwarding header your application sets before the proxy runs, including `X-Real-IP` set by hand before `Do`. A client loses nothing by it: a forwarding header it sends is forwarded whenever `Connection` does not name it.

`proxy.Balancer` takes its `proxy.Config` as an optional variadic argument, like the other middleware constructors. `Servers` (or a custom `Client` with `Clients`) is required, so `proxy.Balancer()` without a config panics at startup, as `proxy.Balancer(proxy.Config{})` does, and so does a `Client` without `Clients`. A server without a port is dialed on the port of its scheme, and each server is reached with its own scheme, so an `https` upstream works behind a plain-HTTP listener.

-The proxy is secure by default. Upstreams that resolve to loopback, private, link-local, multicast, unspecified, CGNAT or other special-use addresses (IPv6 transition forms included) are refused, and so are schemes other than `http` and `https` and HTTPS-to-HTTP redirects. Every request is bounded: `Balancer` buffers at most `MaxResponseBodySize` of an upstream response, 100 MiB unless set (a negative value lifts the bound; a `Config.Client` keeps the bounds of its own clients), and the client behind `Do`, `DoRedirects`, `Forward`, `DomainForward` and `BalancerForward` gives each request, and each redirect hop, 30 seconds for the whole exchange, connect and body included, unless `DoTimeout` or `DoDeadline` set the request's own bound, and buffers at most 100 MiB of a response, until `proxy.WithClient` replaces it. Hop-by-hop headers are stripped, and `Balancer`, `Forward`, `DomainForward` and `BalancerForward` overwrite `X-Real-IP` with `c.IP()`; with `Do`, `DoTimeout`, `DoDeadline` and `DoRedirects` you set it yourself. The trailer section of a chunked request is dropped instead of reaching the upstream as header lines, the trailer section of an upstream's chunked response is dropped instead of reaching the client as header lines, and a forwarding header sent on several lines keeps them in the order they were received; a request carrying more than 64 forwarding lines, the `X-Real-IP` line the proxy writes included, is refused with `431 Request Header Fields Too Large`. To proxy to an internal host, relax the policy with `proxy.WithSecurityPolicy` (or `Config.SecurityPolicy` for `Balancer`), for example `proxy.SecurityPolicy{AllowPrivateIPs: true}`, before you build `DomainForward` or `BalancerForward`: they check their upstreams when the handler is built and panic on a rejected one. Keep the policy installed while they serve: `Forward`, `DomainForward` and `BalancerForward` read it on every request, whereas `Balancer` reads it once, when it is built. See [Security](./middleware/proxy.md#security).
